title: The National Lottery promised billions but good causes ma...
excerpt: Calls for inquiry into how Czech-owned operator Allwyn was awarded licence, amid failure to boost sales and falling revenues
content:
Will the UK winner of the weekend’s £111m EuroMillions jackpot donate any of it to good causes? It would certainly help the National Lottery’s operator, which is facing a black hole of £10bn in the money it raises for community groups, sports organisations and heritage projects.

Grassroots groups face losing out because Allwyn, the Czech-owned operator, has struggled to boost sales since it took over in 2024. There are calls this weekend for an inquiry into the awarding of the lottery licence and the looming funding gap for good causes.

When it won the bid to operate the lottery in 2022, Allwyn UK pledged to deliver £38bn over the 10-year licence to good causes. The company’s ambition has since been scaled back to £60m a week by 2034, or £3.2bn a year, by the end of the licence. Even if it achieves this target, it will be more than £10bn down on the original pledge.

Hugh Robertson, the former chair of the previous lottery operator Camelot and a former Conservative sports minister, said: “Allwyn won the licence on the basis of totally unrealistic predictions on the money that would be raised for good causes. They have failed to deliver.”

Allwyn was formally awarded the fourth National Lottery licence in September 2022 after enlisting Keith Mills, the former chair of the successful London 2012 Olympic campaign, and former Sainsbury’s boss Justin King to galvanise the bid. King is now the chair of Allwyn UK.

‘Allwyn won the licence on the basis of totally unrealistic predictions on the money that would be raised for good causes. They have failed to deliver’

‘Allwyn won the licence on the basis of totally unrealistic predictions on the money that would be raised for good causes. They have failed to deliver’

Hugh Robertson, former Conservative sport minister

The firm, ultimately controlled by Czech billionaire Karel Komárek, promised to “kickstart” the development of a “bigger, better and safer National Lottery”. It said it would recruit new players and promote new games to “capture the imagination” of the nation.

Despite the promise of a rejuvenated lottery during the bid, recent sales have largely flatlined or even fallen. It reflects what appears to be a longer term decline in the lottery’s fortunes, with total UK sales falling by about 25% in real terms from £8.4bn in 2020/21 (now worth £10.6bn after inflation) to £7.9bn in 2025/26.

Of this, money for good causes has averaged at around £1.7bn a year in recent years. But the latest quarterly figures showed a drop to an eight-year low of £377m from April to June – equivalent to £1.5bn a year. Allwyn’s bid claimed it would be more than double that, averaging £3.8bn a year.

A source close to Allwyn said the company’s bid for the licence in 2022 had been designed for a different and less competitive business environment. High-profile draws – such as Omaze promotions to win multimillion pound homes – and other lotteries have since undermined a chunk of the growth envisaged in the bid, said the source.

Allwyn said the drive to increase revenues and overhaul the infrastructure was also initially hampered by unsuccessful litigation from competitors over the bidding process.

Allwyn said despite the challenges, the National Lottery is on track to double the weekly amount of money it raises for good causes. The firm announced this year it had completed a £450m overhaul of the National Lottery and is focused on growth, but there is limited evidence to date of a significant boost in revenues.

In June, Allwyn launched a new version of the flagship Lotto draws on Saturday and Wednesday, with two chances to win in every draw. The prizes for matching three, four or five numbers were reduced.

The website Trustpilot has several reviews of players disgruntled with the new version of Lotto, with complaints about the smaller prizes and struggles in using the National Lottery app. “Absolute awful changes to game,” wrote one user. “How was this takeover allowed?”

Lottery Merseyworld, a website which calculates Lotto revenues from prize structure and distribution, has reported a significant drop in revenues for the game since its launch. Allwyn disputes the figures calculated by Merseyworld, but it does not provide its own figures for sales. The firm declined to answer whether Lotto sales had fallen after the revamp.

Allwyn reported earlier this year that UK gross gaming revenues (sales less prizes) fell in the three months to the end of June to €914m, down 14% on the same quarter the previous year, after stripping out exchange rate fluctuation. The company said a record jackpot roll for Euromillions for the quarter in 2025 had contributed to the year on year decline.

In August, the company announced the unexpected departure of its chief executive, Andria Vidler, with no permanent replacement lined up. The company said that she and King had decided it was the “right time” for her to leave the role, with former William Hill UK managing director Phil Walker appointed interim chief executive.

Media firm Northern and Shell headed by Richard Desmond, which had bid to run the lottery with its bid vehicle the New Lottery Company, challenged the Gambling Commission’s conduct of the competition in the courts, but was unsuccessful. Legal action over the bidding process by Camelot was also dropped, with the firm being acquired by Allwyn.

In its November 2022 report, the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport select committee concluded the commission had overseen “a poorly managed competition”. It warned the Gambling Commission should “vigilantly monitor”Allwyn’s good cause returns to ensure fund distributors were not “short-changed”.

Iain Duncan Smith, the former Conservative party leader, said there needed to be a parliamentary inquiry into the projected returns for good causes and the handling of the bidding process by the Gambling Commission. He said: “They haven’t even achieved the amount that was being given to good causes before they took over. It’s absolutely shocking.”

Allwyn said it had invested in new infrastructure to fulfil its ambition to double weekly returns to good causes to £60m a week by the end of its licence. It said it had overcome the delays to its overhaul caused by legal action.

The firm said: “The high court subsequently confirmed that litigation led to substantial delays, increased costs and loss of revenue for good causes and for Allwyn. We have now completed the biggest transformation in the National Lottery’s history and our focus is firmly on growing participation and increasing returns to good causes.”

The Gambling Commission said: “We remain resolute that we ran a fair and robust competition, and that our evaluation was carried out fairly and lawfully in accordance with our statutory duties. A view shared by the courts in recent legal judgments.”

Officials at the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said that since 2018 returns for good causes have been broadly stable at between £1.6bn and £1.8bn a year and officials regularly review Allwyn’s forecasts, which are shared with lottery distributors.
